title: Introductory Genetics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Biology genetics curriculum: Mendelian inheritance, chromosome theory of heredity, DNA structure and replication basics, non-Mendelian inheritance patterns, sex-linked inheritance, mutation, chromosomal aberrations, linkage, and elementary population genetics.

questions.question: Who is credited as the father of modern genetics, based on his experiments with garden pea plants?
questions.correct_answer: Gregor Mendel
questions.explanation: Gregor Mendel's pea plant experiments in the 1860s established the basic laws of inheritance, earning him the title 'father of genetics'.

questions.question: Mendel's Law of Segregation states that:
options: Genes for different traits assort independently of one another during gamete formation
The two alleles for a gene separate from each other during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele
Dominant alleles always mask recessive alleles completely
Traits are inherited in blended form from both parents
questions.correct_answer: The two alleles for a gene separate from each other during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele
questions.explanation: The Law of Segregation describes how paired alleles separate during meiosis, so each gamete receives only one allele of each gene.

questions.question: The Law of Independent Assortment applies most directly to:
options: Genes located on the same chromosome close together
Genes located on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same chromosome
questions.correct_answer: Genes located on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same chromosome
questions.explanation: Independent assortment holds for genes on separate chromosome pairs (or far apart on one chromosome) because they segregate independently during meiosis; tightly linked genes violate this law.

questions.question: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous (Aa x Aa) individuals, what is the expected phenotypic ratio in the offspring?
questions.explanation: Crossing Aa x Aa produces genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, which gives a 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypic ratio.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross between two individuals heterozygous for two independently assorting genes (AaBb x AaBb), what is the expected phenotypic ratio?
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross of AaBb x AaBb yields four phenotypic classes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio when the two genes assort independently.

questions.question: A test cross is performed by crossing an individual of unknown genotype with:
options: An individual of the same phenotype
questions.correct_answer: A homozygous recessive individual
questions.explanation: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive individual because it reveals the unknown genotype through the phenotypic ratio of the offspring.

questions.question: Which term describes an organism that has two different alleles for a particular gene?
questions.correct_answer: Heterozygous
questions.explanation: Heterozygous describes an individual carrying two different alleles (e.g., Aa) at a given gene locus.

questions.question: The physical appearance or observable characteristics of an organism resulting from its genetic makeup is called its:
questions.correct_answer: Phenotype
questions.explanation: Phenotype refers to the observable traits of an organism, produced by the interaction of its genotype with the environment.

questions.question: In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote phenotype:
options: Is identical to one of the homozygous parents
Shows a blended or intermediate phenotype between the two homozygous parents
Shows both parental phenotypes simultaneously and distinctly
questions.correct_answer: Shows a blended or intermediate phenotype between the two homozygous parents
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote displays a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes, as in pink flowers from red x white crosses.

questions.question: Codominance differs from incomplete dominance in that:
options: Both alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote rather than blending
One allele completely masks the other
The heterozygote phenotype is always intermediate
Codominance only occurs in sex-linked genes
questions.correct_answer: Both alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote rather than blending
questions.explanation: In codominance, such as AB blood type, both alleles are simultaneously and fully expressed, producing a phenotype showing both traits distinctly rather than a blend.

questions.question: The human ABO blood group system is an example of:
options: Simple dominant-recessive inheritance with two alleles
Multiple allelism with codominance between two of the three alleles
questions.correct_answer: Multiple allelism with codominance between two of the three alleles
questions.explanation: The ABO system has three alleles (IA, IB, i) in the population; IA and IB are codominant with each other and both dominant to i.

questions.question: Epistasis refers to a genetic phenomenon in which:
options: Two genes are located on the same chromosome
One gene masks or modifies the phenotypic expression of another, non-allelic gene
A single gene controls multiple unrelated traits
Alleles blend to produce an intermediate phenotype
questions.correct_answer: One gene masks or modifies the phenotypic expression of another, non-allelic gene
questions.explanation: Epistasis occurs when the alleles of one gene locus mask or alter the phenotypic effect of alleles at a different locus, as seen in coat colour determination in some animals.

questions.question: A single gene that affects several apparently unrelated phenotypic traits is said to be exhibiting:
questions.correct_answer: Pleiotropy
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy is the phenomenon where one gene influences multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits, as seen in sickle cell disease affecting red blood cells, organs, and joints.

questions.question: In humans, red-green colour blindness is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous normal. What proportion of their sons will be colour blind?
questions.explanation: Sons receive their X chromosome from the mother, who is homozygous normal, so all sons will be phenotypically normal (though all daughters will be carriers).

questions.question: In humans, sex is normally determined by which chromosome combination in males?
questions.correct_answer: XY
questions.explanation: Human males normally carry one X and one Y chromosome (XY), while females carry two X chromosomes (XX).

questions.question: Haemophilia in humans is an example of a disorder that is:
questions.correct_answer: X-linked recessive
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome, which is why it occurs far more frequently in males than females.

questions.question: The chromosome theory of heredity, proposed largely from the work of Sutton and Boveri and confirmed by Morgan's fruit fly experiments, states that:
options: Genes are carried on chromosomes, which behave in a manner consistent with Mendel's laws
Genes are located only in the cytoplasm
Chromosomes have no role in inheritance
All genes assort independently regardless of chromosome location
questions.correct_answer: Genes are carried on chromosomes, which behave in a manner consistent with Mendel's laws
questions.explanation: The chromosome theory of heredity unified Mendel's abstract 'factors' with the physical behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis, explaining segregation and independent assortment.

questions.question: According to the Watson-Crick model of DNA, adenine pairs with which base, and how many hydrogen bonds form between them?
questions.correct_answer: Thymine, 2 bonds
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine via three hydrogen bonds.

questions.question: DNA replication is described as 'semiconservative' because:
options: Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand
Both strands of the new DNA molecule are entirely new
Only half of the DNA molecule is replicated at a time
Both parental strands remain together in the new molecule
questions.correct_answer: Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand
questions.explanation: Semiconservative replication, demonstrated by Meselson and Stahl, means each daughter DNA molecule retains one parental strand paired with one newly synthesised strand.

questions.question: Which enzyme is primarily responsible for synthesising new DNA strands by adding nucleotides during replication?
questions.correct_answer: DNA polymerase
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase catalyses the addition of complementary nucleotides to a growing DNA strand using the template strand as a guide.

questions.question: During meiosis, crossing over (exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes) occurs during:
questions.correct_answer: Prophase I
questions.explanation: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes occurs during prophase I of meiosis, at the stage when tetrads form and chiasmata become visible.

questions.question: The main biological significance of crossing over during meiosis is that it:
options: Reduces the chromosome number by half
Generates new combinations of alleles, increasing genetic variation
questions.correct_answer: Generates new combinations of alleles, increasing genetic variation
questions.explanation: Crossing over recombines alleles on homologous chromosomes, producing recombinant chromatids and increasing genetic diversity among gametes.

questions.question: Two genes are said to be linked when they:
options: Are located close together on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together
questions.correct_answer: Are located close together on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together
questions.explanation: Linked genes lie near each other on the same chromosome, so they are inherited together more often than predicted by independent assortment, except when separated by crossing over.

questions.question: In genetic mapping, one map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to:
options: A physical distance of exactly 1 micrometre on the chromosome
questions.correct_answer: 1% recombination frequency between two genes
questions.explanation: Genetic map distance is measured in map units (centimorgans), where one map unit equals a 1% recombination frequency between two loci.

questions.question: A change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA is referred to as a:
questions.correct_answer: Mutation
questions.explanation: A mutation is any heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of an organism's DNA, which may arise spontaneously or be induced by mutagens.

questions.question: A frameshift mutation is most likely to be caused by:
options: Substitution of one base for another
Insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three
Silent mutations that do not change the amino acid
questions.correct_answer: Insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three
questions.explanation: Insertions or deletions not in multiples of three shift the reading frame downstream of the mutation, typically altering every subsequent codon and often producing a non-functional protein.

questions.question: Sickle cell anaemia in humans results from:
options: A chromosomal deletion removing the beta-globin gene entirely
A single point mutation in the beta-globin gene causing substitution of valine for glutamic acid
A frameshift mutation in the alpha-globin gene
questions.correct_answer: A single point mutation in the beta-globin gene causing substitution of valine for glutamic acid
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anaemia results from a missense point mutation in the beta-globin gene that substitutes valine for glutamic acid at position 6, altering haemoglobin structure.

questions.question: Down syndrome in humans is caused by:
options: Trisomy of chromosome 21 (three copies instead of two)
A point mutation on the X chromosome
questions.correct_answer: Trisomy of chromosome 21 (three copies instead of two)
questions.explanation: Down syndrome typically results from nondisjunction during meiosis leading to an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).

questions.question: A chromosomal aberration in which a segment of a chromosome is reversed end-to-end is called:
questions.correct_answer: Inversion
questions.explanation: An inversion occurs when a chromosome segment breaks off, flips 180 degrees, and reattaches in the reverse orientation.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome in humans results from the karyotype:
questions.correct_answer: XXY
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome arises from nondisjunction producing males with an extra X chromosome, giving a 47,XXY karyotype.

questions.question: An individual with Turner syndrome has which karyotype?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome results from the presence of only one X chromosome (45,X), typically due to nondisjunction, producing a female with distinctive developmental features.

questions.question: Polyploidy refers to a condition in which an organism has:
options: More than two complete sets of chromosomes
questions.correct_answer: More than two complete sets of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Polyploidy is the possession of three or more complete chromosome sets (e.g., triploid, tetraploid), common in plants and important in crop breeding.

questions.question: A pedigree chart is used in human genetics primarily to:
options: Determine the exact DNA sequence of a gene
Trace the pattern of inheritance of a trait through a family over generations
Measure recombination frequency between two genes
Count the number of chromosomes in a cell
questions.correct_answer: Trace the pattern of inheritance of a trait through a family over generations
questions.explanation: Pedigree analysis uses family trees with standard symbols to track how a trait or disorder is inherited, helping determine its mode of inheritance.

questions.question: In a pedigree, an affected individual whose parents are both unaffected, with the trait skipping generations, most likely indicates the trait is:
questions.correct_answer: Autosomal recessive
questions.explanation: A trait appearing in offspring of unaffected parents, and skipping generations, is characteristic of autosomal recessive inheritance where both parents are unaffected carriers.

questions.question: The Hardy-Weinberg principle predicts that allele and genotype frequencies in a population will remain constant across generations provided that:
options: Mutation, migration, natural selection, and genetic drift are all absent and mating is random
The population undergoes strong natural selection
The population size is very small
questions.correct_answer: Mutation, migration, natural selection, and genetic drift are all absent and mating is random
questions.explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a theoretical baseline requiring no mutation, no migration, no selection, no genetic drift (infinite population), and random mating.

questions.question: Cytoplasmic (extranuclear) inheritance, such as of mitochondrial DNA in humans, typically follows which pattern?
options: Maternal inheritance, since mitochondria are inherited almost exclusively from the egg
Random assortment identical to nuclear genes
questions.correct_answer: Maternal inheritance, since mitochondria are inherited almost exclusively from the egg
questions.explanation: Mitochondria (and their DNA) are passed almost entirely through the cytoplasm of the egg cell, so mitochondrial traits are inherited maternally.

questions.question: In pea plants, Mendel found that the allele for tall stem (T) was dominant to short stem (t). A cross between a homozygous tall plant and a homozygous short plant produces F1 offspring that are:
questions.correct_answer: All tall, heterozygous (Tt)
questions.explanation: Crossing homozygous dominant (TT) with homozygous recessive (tt) produces all heterozygous (Tt) offspring, which display the dominant tall phenotype.
